cases.provenance: A human reviewer flagged this defect in an inline comment on the reviewed pull request.
cases.description:
This can't be right, `dict.get` may return `None` and we don't want to stringify that.

In this case, `CONF_ENTITY_ID` is not optional though, so we should do `[]`, not `.get()`

Same comment for the other constructor parameters.

evidence.thread_resolution:
ThomDietrich: Interesting. I had the same base thought. Every required parameter or optional parameter with a default should exist and be a value, at minimum an empty string "". In the case of unique_id I did not add any conversion because it could indeed be `None`.

I don't get your point with `[]`. The keys exist and the return of `None` isn't solved by it...
ThomDietrich: Had a closer look. Currently the only parameter that can be non-existent is `config.get(CONF_MAX_AGE)`. All the others always exist and are constrained in a certain way and have a value other than `None`.

Of course I agree, this could change at any point and we shouldn't convert None to "None". What now? As the constructor doesn't allow None for most parameters should I add explicit tests in lines above `async_add_entities`? Or should we maybe improve the SCHEMA?

Btw. regarding the empty strings: Check this horrible valid testcase. That shouldn't be allowed, correct?
 https://github.com/home-assistant/core/pull/60997/commits/f908b71de06ce4d5d1dd76a88162e10a78d3db9e
emontnemery: > I don't get your point with []. The keys exist and the return of None isn't solved by it

By doing `[]` (or` __getitem__` really) we assert that the item exists, and if it doesn't, it throws.
We've already validated `config[CONF_ENTITY_ID]` - and all the other configuration variables - so there's no need to stringify.
